versions.text: Criterion: Verify that air vehicle performance information provided to the pilot/operator is accurate to ensure safe flight. Standard: a. Flight manual air vehicle performance for all flight phases including, but not limited to, launch, takeoff, climb, cruise, endurance, maneuver, hover, in-flight refueling, descent, approach, landing, and recovery is sufficiently accurate to allow safe operations. b. Flight manual air vehicle performance includes the full range of mass properties and atmospheric conditions for all air vehicle variants, configurations, and loadings within the flight envelope. c. Air vehicle performance information provided to the pilot/operator by other means (e.g., checklist, calculator, laptop, mission planning tool, onboard embedded system) is sufficiently accurate to allow for safe operation. Method of Compliance: a. An air vehicle force and moment accounting system is defined for all air vehicle variants, configurations, and flight conditions. All coordinate systems, sign conventions, control effectors, aerodynamic and propulsion forces and moments, and aerodynamic/propulsion reference conditions have been defined to support performance simulation. b. Aerodynamic, installed propulsion, and mass properties databases are based on the latest information available, have been placed under configuration control, and are sufficient in scope for all air vehicle configurations, loadings, and flight conditions. All aerodynamic data corrections of the original source analysis/test data to the final, full-scale, flight representative configuration are defined. All propulsion data is corrected for losses and efficiency changes going from uninstalled to installed configurations. Mass properties are representative of all air vehicle configurations and loadings. c. Predictions of trimmed lift and drag in and out of ground effect, installed thrust, power available, power required, fuel flow, fuel quantity, inertias, center of gravity, and weights allow for accurate simulation of air vehicle performance for all atmospheric conditions within the flight envelope. d. Flight manual air vehicle performance is based on simulation models that have been verified against actual air vehicle flight performance and accounts for flight test data measurement uncertainty. e. All flight manual air vehicle performance charts, procedures, and instructions are defined, clearly written, and traceable back to the supporting analysis and data basis. f. Flight manual performance is verified by inspection of documentation. Performance information provided to the pilot/operator by other means is verified against the flight manual or simulation model by test and inspection of documentation. References: JSSG-2001 JSSG-2006 JSSG-2007 MIL-STD-3013 MIL-DTL-7700 MIL-PRF-63029 MIL-DTL-85025 ADS-10-SP ADS-40-SP 14 CFR 23 - Airworthiness Standards: Normal, Utility, Acrobat, and Commuter Category Airplanes 14 CFR 25 - Airworthiness Standards: Transport Category Airplanes 14 CFR 27 - Airworthiness Standards: Normal Category Rotorcraft 14 CFR 29 - Airworthiness Standards: Transport Category Rotorcraft

Standard: The performance information provided to the flight crew is IAW MIL-DTL-7700, Section V – Operating Limitations, Section VI – Flight Characteristics, Section VII – Adverse Weather Operation, Performance Data Appendix/Manual or NAVAIR ACO NATOPS Style Guide, Chapter 4 – Operating Limitations, Part IV – Flight Characteristics and Control Procedures, Part VI – All-Weather Operation, Part XI – Performance Data allowing for mission planning and flight activities within the flight envelope. Method of Compliance: Prior to entering flight test, verify the standard by the following method(s): Examination. (1) Review documentation of the most recent aerodynamic, installed propulsion, and mass properties databases used to develop air vehicle performance. Aerodynamic data covers the full flight envelope for all configurations and loadings. Wind tunnel aerodynamics are corrected for scale effects, support system interference, and geometric differences. Propulsion data is corrected for losses and efficiencies for the air vehicle installed configuration and represents a government approved engine status. Mass properties are representative of all air vehicle configurations and loadings. Databases cover the full up and away flight envelope and takeoff and landing configurations (in and out of ground effect). (2) Review performance information provided to the flight crew to ensure data is available for all phases of flight related to planning and operation (e.g., launch, takeoff, climb, cruise, endurance, maneuver, hover, in-flight refueling, descent, approach, landing, and recovery). (3) Review performance information provided to the flight crew to ensure the data covers the full range of mass properties, operating conditions, and atmospheric conditions for all air vehicle variants, configurations, and loadings within the flight envelope. This includes performance impacts due to icing. (4) Review documentation of the performance analysis, calculations, ground rules, assumptions, and plotting techniques that went into the development of the performance information provided to the flight crew to ensure it complies with MIL-STD-3013, Definitions and General Requirements sections for fixed-wing air vehicles and JSSG-2001, Appendix D, Level III data requirements for rotary-wing air vehicles. (5) Review preliminary performance information provided to the flight crew in other electronic forms (e.g., personal electronic devices, flight management systems, ground control stations, mission planning calculators) to ensure it meets the intent of MIL-DTL-7700, Section V – Operating Limitations section, Section VI – Flight Characteristics section, Section VII – Adverse Weather Operation section, and Performance Data Appendix/Manual section or NAVAIR ACO NATOPS Style Guide, Chapter 4 – Operating Limitations, Part IV – Flight Characteristics and Control Procedures, Part VI – All-Weather Operation, Part XI – Performance Data and complies with MIL-STD-3013, Definitions and General Requirements for fixed-wing vehicles and JSSG- 2001, Appendix D, Level III data requirements for rotary-wing air vehicles. (6) Review preliminary performance information provided to other persons responsible for operation of the air vehicle (e.g., Landing Signal Officer, Catapult Officer) to ensure it complies with MIL-STD-3013, Definitions and General Requirements for fixed-wing air vehicles and JSSG-2001, Appendix D, Level III data requirements for rotary-wing air vehicles. Analysis. (1) Conduct empirical and CFD analysis to build the aerodynamic databases and aerodynamic increments required to determine air vehicle performance. Analysis includes alternate mission equipment, external stores, other configuration variations, impacts due to icing, and other degraded states as applicable. (2) Conduct performance analysis to gather mission, maneuver, airfield takeoff and landing, or ship-based launch and recovery performance information required by the flight crew. Test. (1) Ground test: Conduct all wind tunnel tests necessary to build aerodynamic databases and aerodynamic increments required to determine air vehicle performance. Testing includes alternate mission equipment, external stores, other configuration variations, impacts due to icing, and other degraded states as applicable. Prior to entering operational test/operations, verify the standard by the above and following method(s): Examination. (7) Review flight test reports to assess any updates to the aerodynamic and installed propulsion databases and quantify the resulting air vehicle performance characteristics throughout the full flight envelope for all tested configurations and loadings. (8) Review flight manuals to ensure all performance information is available to the flight crew for all phases of flight related to planning and operation (e.g., launch, takeoff, climb, cruise, endurance, maneuver, hover, in-flight refueling, descent, approach, landing, and recovery). (9) Review flight manuals provided to the flight crew to ensure the data covers the full range of mass properties, operating conditions and atmospheric conditions for all air vehicle variants, configurations, and loadings within the flight envelope. This includes performance impacts due to icing and other degraded states as applicable. (10) Review the performance analysis, calculations, ground rules, assumptions, and plotting techniques that went into the development of the performance information provided in the flight manual to ensure it complies with MIL-STD-3013, Definitions and General Requirements for fixed-wing air vehicles and JSSG-2001, Appendix D, Level III data requirements for rotary-wing air vehicles. (11) Review performance information provided to the flight crew in other electronic forms (e.g., personal electronic devices, flight management systems, ground control stations, mission planning calculators) to ensure it meets the intent of MIL-DTL-7700, Section V – Operating Limitations section, Section VI – Flight Characteristics section, Section VII – Adverse Weather Operation section, and Performance Data Appendix/Manual section or NAVAIR ACO NATOPS Style Guide, Chapter 4 – Operating Limitations, Part IV – Flight Characteristics and Control Procedures, Part VI – All-Weather Operation, Part XI – Performance Data and complies with MIL-STD-3013, Definitions and General Requirements. (12) Review performance information provided to other persons responsible for operation of the air vehicle (e.g., Landing Signal Officer, Catapult Officer) to ensure it complies with MIL-STD- 3013, Definitions and General Requirements for fixed-wing air vehicles and JSSG-2001, Appendix D, Level III data requirements for rotary-wing air vehicles. Test. (2) Flight test: Conduct flight testing to verify and update the aerodynamic and performance characteristics throughout the full flight envelope. Testing should include any alternate mission equipment, external stores, and other configuration variations. Compare flight testing data with modeling analysis and reconcile model with actual flight characteristics. Model reconciliation considers the flight test data quality and instrumentation measurement uncertainty.
